solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Soprano with characteristic sound

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for soprano in music
a characteristic is a distinguishing trait or feature

explanation.surface: A singer is praised for the distinctive quality of her voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like a noun about singing, but here it is the geographical sense: a channel of water.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a sound is a narrow stretch of sea joining two larger bodies of water, as in the Menai Strait.

clue.text: Emperor needs to beat overwhelming sovereignty

indicators.note: overwhelming means one word covers or swamps the other, so it sits around it

parts.note: to tan someone is to beat or thrash them
the Raj was British sovereign rule in India

explanation.surface: A ruler is told he must defeat a rival power that dominates him.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Trajan was a Roman emperor of the second century AD, famous for his column in Rome.

clue.text: Concerned with beauty, I cast thee out!

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are thrown out of order, as a scattered rearrangement

explanation.surface: Someone vain banishes an ugly intruder, as if exorcising a demon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' reads as part of the exorcism cry 'I cast thee out!', but it signals rearranging the letters of I CAST THEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an aesthetic judgement is one about beauty and taste, from the Greek for perception.

clue.text: Saying nothing after Stan drunkenly pockets right change

indicators.note: after places the silent word behind the rest in the answer
pockets means one set of letters takes the other inside it, like a coin in a pocket
drunkenly suggests the letters lurch about into a new order

parts.note: mute means silent, saying nothing

explanation.surface: A tipsy man called Stan quietly slips some change into his pocket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunkenly' gives TANS, which 'pockets' the R; 'after' sets the silent word last. 'change' looks like loose coins but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to transmute something is to change it in form or nature, as alchemists hoped to do with lead.

clue.text: Muddle that is surrounding a new French composer

parts.note: a muddle is a mess

indicators.note: surrounding means one piece goes round the other

parts.note: i.e. (id est) is Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A confused account surrounds some fresh French musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrounding' puts A inside IE to give IAE.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Olivier Messiaen was a twentieth-century French composer known for birdsong-inspired works.

clue.text: So if American returns, ring mobster

indicators.note: returns means the letters go back the way they came, read right to left

parts.note: taken as written
a ring is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: A gangster threatens: if the American comes back, call me.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns SO IF AM round to MAFIOS, and O is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a mafioso is a member of the Mafia, the archetypal organised-crime gangster.

clue.text: Tired of Street-Porter?

parts.note: porter is a dark beer, a kind of ale

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether we are weary of Janet Street-Porter, the British broadcaster and journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: Janet Street-Porter is a British TV presenter; the hyphenated name is split into its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: stale means tired in the sense of jaded or worn out from overfamiliarity.

clue.text: Intimate meal with no starter

indicators.note: with no starter means the first letter is dropped, playing on a meal without its first course

parts.note: dinner is a meal

explanation.surface: A cosy dinner for two skips the first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no starter' drops the D from DINNER; the culinary 'starter' is the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: inner feelings are private and intimate, kept close to oneself.

clue.text: Earl messed up, taping last bit of Antony and Cleopatra?

indicators.note: messed up means the letters are jumbled into another order
last bit of picks out the final letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A nobleman bungles recording the final scene of Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'messed up' jumbles the tape word with the Y that 'last bit of' takes. 'Antony and Cleopatra' looks like one title; only Cleopatra is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Cleopatra was queen of Egypt, so she is an instance of an Egyptian; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Fat knight's first to swim in a couple of rivers

definitions.note: the clue reads 'Fat knight is', the definition plus a link

indicators.note: in places the letter inside the other piece

parts.note: the Fal in Cornwall and the Taff in Wales are two British rivers

indicators.note: first to picks the opening letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A heavy knight is the first to take a swim across two rivers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first to' picks S from swim; 'in' sets it between the Cornish river and the Welsh one.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Sir John Falstaff is Shakespeare's corpulent, roguish knight in Henry IV and The Merry Wives of Windsor.

clue.text: Sent back section of glossy on nasty bugs

indicators.note: Sent back says the hidden letters are read backwards
section of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone returns a piece of shiny magazine that has unpleasant insects on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'section of' takes SYONNA from glossY ON NAsty, and 'Sent back' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something that bugs you irritates or pesters you, an informal sense of the verb.

clue.text: British mountain provides disappointment

parts.note: Mount Athos is a holy mountain in northern Greece

explanation.surface: A climber finds a British peak an anticlimax.
explanation.definitionFit: Literary sense: bathos is an abrupt drop from the elevated to the trivial, an anticlimactic letdown.

clue.text: Estimate too highly the frequency of deliveries?

definitions.meaning: to value or judge something above its worth
in cricket the ... is how quickly a fielding side bowls its overs of six balls

explanation.surface: An analyst warns against overestimating how often parcels arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a bowler's balls are 'deliveries', grouped into overs; the over rate measures how many overs are bowled per hour.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the verb means judge too favourably, and split in two the words name cricket's rate of bowling overs.

clue.text: Regularly arrange student charity event

indicators.note: regularly means taking letters at even intervals, here every second one

explanation.surface: An organiser routinely sets up a college fundraiser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' takes the second, fourth and sixth letters of aRrAnGe.
explanation.definitionFit: British usage: a rag is a university students' charity fundraising event or week, often with stunts and parades.

clue.text: Hit out at sound that's repetitive

indicators.note: hit suggests the letters are knocked about into a new order

parts.note: a sound argument is logical, well reasoned

explanation.surface: Someone lashes out at a noise that keeps repeating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit' rearranges OUT AT into TAUTO; 'sound' is the adjective, not a noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: tautological statements say the same thing twice in different words, so they are needlessly repetitive.

clue.text: Met patron perhaps, since in Queens after work

indicators.note: after puts the second part behind the first in the answer

parts.note: OP (opus) is the abbreviation for a musical work

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside the other

parts.note: ER (Elizabeth Regina) is a queen; two of them give ERER
ago means since, back in time, as in long ago

explanation.surface: A New Yorker from the borough of Queens has been going to the Met since finishing work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' nests the word for since between two queens; 'after' places all that behind the work. The Met is New York's Metropolitan Opera; Queens looks like the borough.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: someone who attends performances at the Metropolitan Opera is a patron of opera houses.

clue.text: Soccer team compete with audience

parts.note: Inter is Inter Milan, the Italian football club
to vie is to compete

explanation.surface: A football club competes in front of a crowd of spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'audience' looks like spectators; here it is a formal meeting, as in an audience with the Pope.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an audience is a formal hearing or meeting with someone important, a kind of formal interview.

clue.text: Ripped invite up — that's harsh

indicators.note: ripped suggests the letters are torn up and reassembled in another order

explanation.surface: Someone tears up an invitation, a harsh snub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ripped' rearranges INVITE UP; 'up' belongs to the letters, not to 'ripped up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: punitive measures are intended to punish, so they are severe or harsh.

clue.text: Spam? Dodgy mail I deleted on cue then

indicators.note: dodgy means suspect or unsound, so the letters are reshuffled
deleted says the named letter is removed from the word before it

explanation.surface: Junk email is deleted at the right moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deleted' removes I from MAIL to leave MAL; 'Dodgy' rearranges MAL with ON CUE THEN. Spam looks like junk email but is the tinned meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Spam is a brand of tinned pork, the best-known processed meat of its kind; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Maybe Balmoral talks will be endless

indicators.note: endless means both outer letters are cut off the word

parts.note: chats are talks

explanation.surface: Royal discussions at the Scottish castle of Balmoral will go on for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' cuts C and S from CHATS. Balmoral looks like the royal castle but is also a flat Scottish bonnet.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a balmoral is a brimless Scottish bonnet, a kind of headwear; 'Maybe' marks the example.

clue.text: Note a bouquet is budding

parts.note: a wine's bouquet is its scent

explanation.surface: A florist observes that a bunch of flowers is just coming into bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bouquet' looks like flowers but is the aroma, as of wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something nascent is just coming into being, like a budding talent.

clue.text: Austerity in dress runs for short time

indicators.note: for means one letter takes the place of another

parts.note: a rig-out is an outfit of clothes
T is the abbreviation for time
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Wartime austerity in clothing lasts only briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' swaps R in place of the T of RIGOUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: rigour means strictness or severity, close to austerity in its sense of harsh self-discipline.

clue.text: Clothes for trendy people

definitions.meaning: low-slung trousers that sit on the hips rather than the waist
fashionable young people who follow the latest cultural trends

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: low-waisted trousers worn on the hips, and the fashion-conscious young who chase what is cool.

clue.text: Tot is grabbed by wings of shore bird

indicators.note: is grabbed by means the first piece is held inside the second
wings of picks the two outermost letters of the next word

parts.note: a nip and a tot are both small measures of spirits

explanation.surface: A small child is snatched up by the wings of a seabird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wings of' gives S and E from shore; 'is grabbed by' puts NIP between them. 'shore bird' reads together but only 'bird' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the snipe is a long-billed wading bird of marshes and wetlands.

clue.text: Avoid kid, missing first daughter

indicators.note: missing first means the opening letter is taken away

parts.note: to kid someone is to delude or fool them

explanation.surface: Steer clear of a child, leaving out the eldest girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kid' looks like a child but is the verb, to fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to elude is to avoid or escape, as a fugitive slips past pursuers.

clue.text: Nowadays cobblers will keep one handy

parts.note: AD (anno domini) marks the present era

indicators.note: will keep means one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: cobblers is British slang for nonsense, rot
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Modern shoe-menders will keep a useful tool handy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cobblers' looks like shoemakers but is British slang for rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: adroit means skilful and dexterous, handy with one's hands.

clue.text: Mike needs one place setting

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet
I is the Roman numeral for one
lieu is French for place, as in 'in lieu of'

explanation.surface: A man named Mike requires one table setting at dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'place setting' reads as cutlery for one; 'place' and 'setting' work separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a milieu is a social setting or environment in which someone lives.

clue.text: Poet penning chapter on the end of George Smiley?

indicators.note: on means placed after, written on top of what comes before in a down-style charade
the end of picks the final letter of the word that follows
penning means enclosing, like an animal in a pen

parts.note: Andrew Motion was Poet Laureate of the UK

explanation.surface: A poet writes a chapter about the end of George Smiley, le Carré's spy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penning' puts C into MOTION; 'on' puts that after E from 'the end of' George. George Smiley is John le Carré's spymaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a smiley face such as :-) is an emoticon, a symbol made of keyboard characters.

clue.text: Violent English border guards let out? On the contrary

indicators.note: guards means one piece encloses another protectively
On the contrary reverses the stated roles, so the second piece encloses the first

parts.note: to vent is to let out, as feelings or steam
a hem is the border of a garment

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a fierce English border guard was set free.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, 'guards' would put let out inside English border; 'On the contrary' flips the roles, so let out goes round EHEM.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: vehement means forceful and intense, close to violent in the sense of passionate fury.

clue.text: Repay one signing cheque on return

indicators.note: on return means the word comes back the other way, read right to left

parts.note: the drawer of a cheque is the person who signs it

explanation.surface: A person who writes a cheque is paid back when it comes back to them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on return' turns DRAWER round.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to reward someone is to repay them for a service or kindness.
